newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar-Thai premiums firm, eye on Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar-Thai premiums firm, eye on Taiwan.

text.p: Thai sugar premiums firmed this week after the New York market's spot month expiry, and attention was on a Taiwan tender result of 30,000 tonnes raw sugar, sugar traders in Asia said on Wednesday.
Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery quoted at 0.65/0.70 cents per pound (bid/offer) over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on a free on board (FOB) basis.
July/September deliveries were quoted at 0.57/0.65 cents. Traders said that the July/September premiums gained in line with the May/July.
"South Africa and Australia will start exporting raw sugar from next month. Their smooth shipments will determine Thai premiums in the near term," a sugar trader at a major trade house in Japan said.

State-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp on April 23 passed on a 30,000-tonne raw sugar tender due to high bid prices at a tender in New York City. The shipment was slated for June 5 to June 20 arrival to Taiwan.
The shipment would be re-tendered on May 6 with the same specifications, and the tender result will be announced on Wednesday.
A Japanese trade house is involved with the tender, seeking to send Thai raw sugar to Taiwan, Tokyo traders said.
Hong Kong traders said the result of the Taiwan tender, expected around 0600 GMT, could surprise the market.
Japan's total raw sugar imports in the first three months of this year were 241,544 tonnes, against 287,909 tonnes during the same period of last year.
China had sold three to four cargoes of 13,000 to 14,000 tonnes of white sugar to Pakistan for June delivery at around $370 per tonne, C&F Karachi.
"The quality is better than Thai or Brazilian, and that brand is quite popular in Pakistan," said one sugar trader.
Others said that Pakistan preferred Chinese packing, along with bigger grains and drier sugar and were, for the moment, willing to pay up to a $10-dollar premium for it.
The Pakistan government earlier this week decided to abolish a 10 percent import duty on sugar to guard against any shortages.
Some Hong Kong traders said the measure could not last long as Pakistan sugar mills would agitate to protect their domestic market.

Hong Kong and China traders were usure how much more Chinese sugar Pakistan would import, with price seen as the main factor. "We expect Pakistan to import (a total of) about one million tonnes of sugar this year," said a China-based trader.
There was also some interest in Chinese sugar from the Middle East, but enquiries had not materialised into deals as a new Saudi sugar mill was expected to start production in July, the trader said.
The price of white sugar in China's sugar producing province of Guangxi was slightly firmer at 3,900 yuan per tonne ($470) and traders said they were slightly more bullish on prices.
But others said that Chinese sugar futures had dropped and that some companies were selling futures and buying physical.
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto in Tokyo (813) 3432 7391
-- Mishi Saran in Hong Kong (852) 2843 6358
